messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Imran Khan had spent most of his adult life around danger, but the event that marked him came in the sterile brightness of a children’s ward, not on a worksite. His eight-year-old son had been admitted with a sudden, life-threatening illness, and Imran remembered the unbearable hours in which he stood beside a bed crowded with drips, tubing, and needles, while the air carried that sharp hospital smell that seemed to cling to his clothes long after he left. He had expected to be useful, steady, capable of acting under pressure, as he was in his job as a bomb disposal technician. Instead, he found himself watching the monitors, listening to every sound in the corridor, and feeling his body lock into alertness as if he had to stay awake forever to stop something worse from happening. What has haunted him since is not a verbal account but a series of pictures: the pale sheet over his son’s chest, the line of the IV, the flash of a nurse’s hands, the look on his child’s face. When those images return, they do so without warning and with a force that makes the room around him disappear; he experiences them as if he is back there, with the antiseptic smell, the metallic sight of medical equipment, and the same sick dread all at once.

In the months afterward, anything that carried that ward into the present could seize him. The smell of a clinic corridor, the sight of needles or a drip stand in a pharmacy, even being near children at a park or at family gatherings, could abruptly bring the whole memory back, and he would be caught in it before he understood what had set it off. These moments were followed by strong physical reactions—his chest tightening, his pulse racing, his body bracing—and by an instant sense that he had to stay on guard, because he had come to believe that if he ever relaxed, he might miss the next sign of disaster. That fear of missing danger kept him from falling asleep easily; nights became a kind of watchfulness in which he lay awake listening to every sound in the house. He also began to read the reactions themselves as proof that something was badly wrong with him. Imran was ashamed of how frightened he felt, and he had come to believe he was weak, that a man who had handled explosives for years should not be reduced by a hospital room, and that the way his body seized up meant he was going crazy. At the same time, he felt helpless before the memory of his son’s illness and certain that he could not stop bad things from happening, no matter how hard he tried.

The more those pictures returned, the more his certainty deepened. Each unbidden flashback seemed to tell him that the danger was still near and that he was powerless in the face of it. Once he was back in the grip of the memory, his fear and shame intensified, and he would notice hospital smells or the sight of medical equipment even more sharply, scanning for them in places where other people would not think to look. He started avoiding children’s wards, waiting rooms, and errands that might require him to pass through a hospital entrance. At work, he found himself tense even in ordinary settings, and he disliked being sent near a clinic or emergency site in case the smell or sight of equipment set off another surge. The avoidance was not just of places but of anything that might invite the same helplessness back into his body; yet the more he rearranged his routes, his sleeping, and his daily movements, the more narrow his world became. He noticed that when he was already on edge, the smallest reminder—a child’s voice in a supermarket aisle, a glimpse of a syringe in a poster, the faint trace of antiseptic on someone’s clothes—could trigger the same flood of images and sensations. That left him feeling even more weak and trapped, and the belief that he could not protect his family fed his need to monitor his surroundings at all times.

By the time he sought help, Imran was exhausted from living as if disaster were always moments away. He came in at his wife’s urging after another night of lying awake, listening for trouble, and after he had caught himself pulling away from grandchildren because their presence made him feel sick with fear. He is most afraid that these reactions mean he is losing his mind and becoming unable to function, but he is also hoping that if he can understand why the ward, the smell, the needles, and the sight of children still catch him so powerfully, he may finally be able to sleep again and feel less ruled by the memory of his son’s illness.
